8.4 — Boss Attacks: Patterns & Phases

The boss can be hurt (8.3) and does not care. Today it starts answering. You are going to build the two attacks your spec promised, give each one a telegraph the player can read, and move every timing number into a phase table so that Phase 3 is a change of values rather than a rewrite. The boss has no attacks in this project yet, and no projectile of its own — everything here is assembled from the pieces you have already built once.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I give a boss two attacks and a phase table?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

The boss can be hurt and it does not answer back. Give it two attacks — one that travels across the arena and one that is its own body — and hold every timing number in a phase table, so Phase 3 is a change of values rather than a rewrite. As one problem it is not startable: an attack is three timed beats, and neither attack exists in this project yet.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Name the three beats, and give each one a numberwhat does this part do?Read: the three-beat table in this lesson's first activity, and the fight arithmetic you wrote in 8.1
  2. Build the travelling attack as a prefab of its ownwhat does this part do?Read: 3.2 — Projectiles: Instantiate, Fire, Destroy, and its Tinker on bullet tuning: the muzzle offset, the heading, the speed knob and the lifetime
  3. Re-point the damage at the playerwhat does this part do?Read: the damage knob you declared on the projectile in 3.4, and the refactor that moved TakeDamage onto StatManager.Instance in 5.3
  4. Build the body attack out of the chase comparison you already ownwhat does this part do?Read: 4.3 — Chase: The Aggro Radius (the comparison that names a direction), and 4.4 for the contact damage the charge deals
  5. Decide what schedules the attack — and what stops itwhat does this part do?Read: the scheduling table in this lesson, and the state machine you built in 4.5
  6. Hold the numbers in a phase table, and read the row on phase entrywhat does this part do?Read: the phase-value table in this lesson, and the guarded phase entry you wrote in 8.2

Every part above is a problem you have already solved once, pointed at a new target: part two is your own bullet, part four is your own chase, part five is your own state machine, and part six is 8.2's guard with a table behind it. The genuinely new part is the first one — deciding the numbers before writing them — because the player experiences an attack as a length of time, not as a line of code. Get the split right and the code is transcription.

The test for a finished split: does the part name something you could point at — a prefab, a field, a method, a row of a table? "Make the boss attack" points at nothing. "Where the travelling attack is spawned" points at one line in one method, and that is a part.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Both attacks need a telegraph and a recovery, and only one of them needs a heading. Which part above carries the difference between them — and what does that tell you about how much of the second attack is genuinely new?

Pick one number from your table that must never change between phases, and say what the fight stops being if it does.

The Problem: An Unreadable Attack Is Not an Attack ~10 min

A boss that damages you is trivial to build: put a number on a timer and subtract health. That boss is also unplayable, because the player's only possible response is to take the hit and hope. Every good attack is a sentence with three parts, and all three are timing, not geometry:

BeatWhat the boss is doingWhat the player is doingWhat the designer fixes
Telegraph Announcing the attack — a wind-up pose, a colour flash, a sound, a rearing back. Reading it, and starting the correct response. How long the tell lasts. Too short and the fight is unfair; too long and it is boring. This is the single most important number in the fight.
Strike Committing — the wave travels, the body charges. Executing the answer: jumping, sidestepping, or already being somewhere else. What the answer is, and whether the answer is physically possible. Your spec's counterplay sentence lives or dies here.
Recovery Unable to act — the boss is committed and vulnerable. Attacking. This is where the player's damage comes from. How long the boss is helpless. This number, more than any other, sets the pace of the whole fight.

Notice what that table implies: the player's damage window is the boss's recovery time. If you never give the boss a recovery, you have built a fight where the only correct move is to run, and the only reason you win is patience. Read your 8.1 spec again with that in mind — every attack you wrote has a recovery, whether you wrote one down or not.

What you already own. You built a turret in Unit 3 that detects the player by distance and fires projectiles on a fire-rate cooldown, and a projectile that spawns, travels, damages what it touches and destroys itself. That is the boss's ranged attack, wearing a different costume. You built an enemy in Unit 4 with a patrol / chase / attack state machine. That is the boss's charge. Nothing in this lesson is a new idea — it is your own code, re-pointed at a new target.

Socratic: Why Timing Is the Whole Design

  1. Write your spec's first attack as three numbers: telegraph seconds, strike seconds, recovery seconds. What is the player's damage window, expressed as one of those three?
  2. If the telegraph is shorter than a human's reaction time, what is the attack actually testing — skill, or luck? Look up a typical human reaction time and compare it to your number.
  3. If the recovery is longer than the telegraph, what does the fight become? Name a game you have played that does this deliberately.
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

A telegraph is a promise made in advance. These five come from worlds where being early is the difference between a warning and an incident.

Example 1 — A level crossing (the barrier drops long before the train arrives):

// The barrier comes down eight seconds before the train. The eight
// seconds is not slack - it is the whole safety system.

Example 2 — A stage manager's cue call (a warning that is also an instruction):

// "Standby LX 12... LX 12 GO." The standby is the telegraph;
// the GO is the strike. The operator is never surprised.

Example 3 — Artillery ranging (one slow shot before the real one):

// The first round is deliberately slow and obvious so the crew can
// adjust. It is not wasted - it is the telegraph.

Example 4 — A press interlock (the cycle cannot be interrupted, only entered):

// Once the press cycle starts it completes. The operator's only
// decision was made before the cycle began.

Example 5 — A two-minute warning (the same event, announced earlier each time):

// Same warning, same meaning, but the window to react is smaller.
// That is how a sport escalates without changing its rules.

Predict Before Building

  1. Example 5 escalates by shrinking the window without changing the rules. Which of your three beats will Phase 3 shorten, and what is the floor below which it must not go?
  2. Example 4 says the decision is made before the cycle begins. In your boss's charge, at what exact moment is the player's decision made — and can they change their mind after it?
  3. Example 1's eight seconds is a fixed, knowable number. Does the player need to know the number, or only to see the barrier move? What does that tell you about whether your telegraph should be a timer or a visual?
Read the Docs: Three Ways to Schedule an Attack ~15 min

"The boss attacks every three seconds" can be built at least three ways. All three are legitimate, and they are not equally expensive to change later. Pick one and defend it.

ApproachWhat it looks likeWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) A timer in Update A float holding the last attack time, compared against Time.time. Exactly the shape you used for the turret's fire rate in 3.3. Every attack's state now lives in one method, and the boss will happily fire while it is mid-charge, mid-death, or after the player is gone, unless you guard each case. You have one attack and want it working in ten minutes.
(b) A coroutine A method that waits, telegraphs, strikes, recovers, and loops — reading top to bottom like the attack itself. You must keep a handle on it to stop it, or the boss keeps attacking after it dies. And an interrupted coroutine leaves the boss in whatever pose it was in. Your attack is a strict sequence of timed beats and you want the code to read like the timeline.
(c) A state machine The pattern you already built in 4.5: an enum, one state per frame, and transitions on conditions. Telegraph, Strike, Recover become three states. The most structure up front, and the most places to get a transition wrong. You want "the boss is vulnerable during recovery" to be a property of the machine rather than a flag you remember to set — and you already know how to write one.

And separately: where do the numbers live? A phase change is not a behaviour change, it is a change of values. There are three ways to hold those values, and the cheapest one to tune is rarely the one people pick first:

ApproachWhat it looks likeWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) Reassign fields on phase entry The phase entry method assigns new values to attack interval, movement speed and so on, depending on which phase it is. The numbers are buried in code, so tuning Phase 3 means editing a script rather than a value. Two phases with the same value must both be written out. You have two phases, three numbers, and a deadline.
(b) A table indexed by phase One array or list of small records — one row per phase, one column per number — and a single reader that looks up the current phase's row. You must design the row's shape before you know all the columns you need, and changing that shape later touches every row. You can see the whole difficulty curve in one place, side by side, and tune it by comparing rows.
(c) One asset per phase A Unity ScriptableObject asset for each phase, holding that phase's numbers and referenced by the boss. A whole new kind of Unity asset to learn, and three files to keep straight on disk. You want a designer to tune the fight in the Inspector without opening the code at all.

Choose, Then Justify

  1. Which scheduling approach did you choose, and which of the three costs did you accept?
  2. If you chose a coroutine, what stops it when the boss dies? What is the visible symptom in the scene if you forget?
  3. If you chose a state machine, name the three or four states and write the transition condition on each arrow. Which arrow is the one the player is watching for?
Build Lab: Two Attacks and a Phase Table ~30 min

Attack 1 — the travelling attack. Most specs have one. Build it the way you built your turret's projectile in 3.2: spawn it, let it travel, damage what it touches, destroy it on contact or after a lifetime. You already solved every one of those problems once. Two things are different, and both are yours to fix:

  • Nothing in this project is this attack yet. You are creating a new prefab. Do not assume a starting point exists — the Turret_Projectile prefab in Assets/Prefabs carries no collider, so even reusing it means adding one yourself, and its script is an empty file. Your own working projectile from Unit 3 is the better starting point.
  • The target is the player, not the boss. Your turret's projectile already damages the player through the signed-amount damage method your StatManager owns — the number you moved there in 5.3. Confirm which tag it checks before you re-point anything.

The whole thing reduces to three beats and one method that sets its heading:

public void Initialize(Vector2 direction)   // spawner sets the heading; the
                                            // projectile does not guess
// then: travel, damage on contact, destroy - all three you have written before

Choose the speed from your own numbers. There is no projectile speed to copy in this project — read the value you chose for your turret's projectile in 3.2. Your boss's attack should be slower, because it is a rhythm the player has to step out of, not a bullet they have to already be clear of. Then check the height against your jump: the player's apex, from 6.1, has to clear the attack's collider with room to spare. If it does not, one of those two numbers is wrong.

Attack 2 — the body attack. The boss's own collider is the weapon: it announces itself, commits to a direction, moves fast for a short time, then is helpless while it recovers. The direction is the same comparison your enemy's chase already makes in 4.3, flattened to one axis because the arena is flat. The recovery is the state where the player finally gets to use 8.3.

Architectural specification: the attack the player must be able to answer.
  • What exactly does the player see during the telegraph? Name it as a thing on screen, not a variable.
  • How long is the telegraph, in seconds, and how does that compare to a human reaction time? What is the player expected to do in that window — start moving, or already be moving?
  • What is the counterplay sentence, with numbers in it: "the player ___s; it works because the attack is ___ and their ___ is ___."
  • What does a mistake cost, in the player's own health — and what fraction of their maximum health is that? If the answer is "most of it", the fight allows almost no mistakes and your spec's fight length is a fantasy.
  • During the recovery, the boss is vulnerable. How long is that window, and how many swings does 8.3's cooldown fit inside it? If the answer is less than one, the player can never land a hit and the fight cannot be won.
Architectural specification: the phase table.
  • List every number that changes per phase: attack interval, travel speed, telegraph length, recovery length, movement speed. Which of those must not change, no matter what?
  • Where is that table stored, and how does the boss read the row for its current phase?
  • Which numbers change at Phase 2, and which at Phase 3? If a number changes at both, why does it need two steps rather than one?
  • Phase 3 adds a new attack as well as faster numbers. What in your table says "this attack is available from phase 3" — and what happens if you forget that guard?
  • The phase entry from 8.2 is guarded so it fires once. Does your table read happen there, or every frame? What is the cost of the wrong choice?
The boss will keep attacking after it dies unless something stops it. This is the classic coroutine and timer bug: the death path destroys the object or stops the health logic, but the attack scheduler is running on its own and does not know. Watch for a wave that spawns from the boss's last position a second after the boss is gone. The fix is a guard on the scheduler, not a longer delay.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name the three beats of an attack and say which one is the player's damage window
  • Defend your choice of scheduling approach, and say what one of the other two would have cost you
  • Explain how the body attack reuses your own enemy chase logic, and how the travelling attack reuses your own projectile
  • Say the counterplay sentence for each attack with real numbers in it, including your own jump height and walk speed
  • Explain what the phase table changes and what it must never change
  • Beat your own boss, and quote the fight time
  • Break this feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this feature came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
